title: Apportionment methods in resource allocation
abstract: The efficient use of human resources. We are considering an organization with a fixed number of workers over a network of subunits. The relative efficiency of these units can be uncovered using Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) methods. How do we overcome efficiency differences when resources are constrained? Motivated by concerns for quality assurance, we use a method that lexico-graphically minimizes the tasks per worker. We present a fast algorithm to calculate the optimal allocation. Connections to the apportionment literature — mostly focusing on the fair allocation of voting districts among geographical or administrative regions, — are discussed. The method is illustrated using data from salary administrators at the Hungarian State Treasury's 19 county-level subsidiaries. After the reallocation, the relative efficiency of the worst-performing counties moves from about 60% to over 90%.
summary_en: How should an organisation distribute a fixed number of workers across operationally heterogeneous subunits when units differ in efficiency? Kóczy, Koltai and Sziklai propose using apportionment methods — classically used to allocate parliamentary seats — adapted to resource allocation. They develop a leximin (lexicographic min-max) method that minimises tasks per worker and provide a fast algorithm. Applied to salary administrators at the Hungarian State Treasury's 19 county-level subsidiaries, the optimal reallocation raises the worst-performing county's relative efficiency from ~60% to over 90% without adding staff.
data_used: Hungarian State Treasury (MÁK) administrative data on standard administrative tasks per month for each of the 19 county-level subsidiaries; covers worker headcount and task volume for multiple years.
policy_relevance: Direct, immediately applicable to the Hungarian State Treasury (MÁK) and other multi-site Hungarian public bodies (NAV regional offices, NEAK county branches, KSH regional units). The leximin algorithm provides a transparent, fairness-justifiable method for relocating staff to equalise workloads. Already validated on actual MÁK data with measurable efficiency gains.
